overview.title: 📖 Overview: The Textures of Public Space
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 7a–7b
overview.hebrewSource: אֵין כַּרְמְלִית פְּחוּתָה מֵאַרְבָּעָה, וְתוֹפֶסֶת עַד עֲשָׂרָה
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Daf 7 examines the fine grain of what makes a space public, private, or something in between. It opens with the karpef, a large fenced enclosure that is a genuine Torah-level private domain despite the Sages treating it more strictly because no one lives there, and works outward from there to marginal urban spaces — a street corner, the gap between pillars, a merchant's bench — each a karmelit because its use, though real, is inconvenient. The Gemara then measures exactly how tall and how wide a protrusion in the public domain must be to count as part of it, sets the outer boundaries of karmelit status itself, and closes with Abaye's ruling about digging out a pit to complete a low-ceilinged house into a full private domain, and the resulting dispute over whether 'holes' in the public domain share its status.

slides.title: 🌾 The Karpef: A True Private Domain, Restricted Anyway
slides.subtitle: A large fenced enclosure not built for residence

boxes.title: By Torah Law
items: A karpef larger than a beit se'atayim, fenced but not built for residence — even the size of a kor or two
One who throws an object into it from the public domain is liable, because it has real partitions

boxes.title: By Rabbinic Law
items: Because it lacks residents, the Sages restricted carrying inside it as though it were a karmelit
This rabbinic leniency does not undo its Torah-level status as a private domain

boxes.title: A Reading Dispute
items: Ulla explains the mishna's 'valley' via this karpef concept — but then why would the mishna call it a 'valley' rather than an enclosure?
Rav Ashi instead reads the mishna's own words literally: it says 'private domain,' so he needs no such explanation

callout.label: Underlying idea:
callout.text: Partitions create a private domain by Torah law regardless of whether anyone lives there — but the Sages still layer on restrictions where ordinary residential use is missing.

slides.title: 🚶 Degrees of Inconvenient Use
slides.subtitle: Marginal urban spaces that fall short of a full public domain
rows: Corner adjacent to the public domain (קֶרֶן זָוִית)
Crowds occasionally push in, but its use is inconvenient
Between the pillars alongside the public domain
Multitudes stride there, but not in a direct, unbroken path
The bench before the pillars (אִיצְטְבָא), for merchants' wares
Karmelit — by some accounts, even more clearly so
Its use is less convenient still than the space between the pillars

callout.label: Why it matters:
callout.text: This is precisely why the Tosefta's list of domains names 'karmelit' as its own category, beyond sea, valley, and colonnade — to capture these marginal, semi-used urban spaces.

slides.title: 🧱 What Counts as Public Domain?
slides.subtitle: Measuring exactly how a protrusion in the street is treated

steps.content: 1️⃣ An upright brick in the public domain: an object thrown and stuck to its side makes one liable — the side is treated as part of the public domain itself
2️⃣ An object landing atop the brick is exempt, so long as the brick is at least three handbreadths high — the multitudes don't step on top of it
3️⃣ Thorns and shrubs are never part of the public domain, even under three handbreadths high, since people avoid walking on them
4️⃣ Feces in the roadway: disputed — Chiyya bar Rav says it is not part of the public domain since people avoid it; Rav Ashi says it IS, since people rushing to work step on it anyway

callout.label: Underlying test:
callout.text: Every case turns on the same question: does the ordinary crowd actually tread there, or not?

slides.title: 📏 The Karmelit's Boundaries
slides.subtitle: How wide, and how high, a karmelit can be
rows: A space narrower than four handbreadths cannot become a karmelit — it is a mere exempt domain instead
Rav Sheshet's qualification of Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
A karmelit 'extends up to 10' handbreadths high
Above ten handbreadths, an area is no longer treated as a karmelit at all
Shmuel to Rav Yehuda: 'do not get involved in Shabbat questions above ten handbreadths'
A roofless house (walls under 10, roof completes it to 10)
On the roof: a full private domain, carry anywhere. Inside: karmelit-like, limited to 4 cubits
Cited to test whether the height rule is really about the karmelit itself

callout.label: Borrowed leniencies:
callout.text: The Sages built the karmelit from pieces of both other domains: like a private domain, it needs an area of 4×4 to exist at all; like a public domain, its reach tops out at 10 handbreadths.

slides.title: 🕳️ Holes of a Domain
slides.subtitle: Abaye's dug-out pit, and a dispute over holes in the public domain

lines.speaker: Abaye
lines.text: If one digs a pit of four by four handbreadths in the floor of that roofless house, completing its depth to ten handbreadths, the WHOLE house becomes fit for carrying.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Why? Because the dug-out spot is itself a private domain, and the rest of the house becomes its 'holes' (חוֹרֵי רְשׁוּת הַיָּחִיד) — and everyone agrees holes of a private domain share its status.

lines.speaker: Abaye
lines.text: The same logic should extend to holes of the public domain — treat them as public domain too.

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: No — holes of the public domain are NOT like the public domain itself. Its holes are governed by whether their use is convenient, the same test that makes a street corner only a karmelit.

callout.label: Rava's consistency:
callout.text: This matches his earlier reasoning — a corner adjacent to the public domain stays a karmelit specifically because its use is inconvenient, proving that mere proximity to RH does not automatically confer RH status.

summary.principle: Torah-level domain status depends on real partitions and genuine, convenient public use — a fenced karpef is a true private domain despite lacking residents, marginal spaces like corners and pillar-gaps remain only a karmelit, and the karmelit itself is bounded between four and ten handbreadths.

flowSteps.content: 🌾 A karpef is a Torah-level private domain by its partitions, though the Sages restrict it like a karmelit for lacking residents
🚶 Corners, pillar-gaps, and merchants' benches remain karmelit — used, but not conveniently
🧱 A street-level protrusion counts as public domain only where the crowd actually treads on it

columns.content: 📏 Karmelit status requires an area of 4×4, and tops out at 10 handbreadths high
🕳️ Holes of a private domain share its status; holes of a public domain are disputed

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: what makes a space public, private, or karmelit is measured by real partitions and genuine, convenient use — not mere proximity or occasional passage

quiz.q: What is a karpef, and why is it still a true private domain by Torah law despite the Sages restricting it?
o: A small basket; it is exempt because it is under 4×4 handbreadths
A large fenced enclosure not built for residence; it has genuine partitions, so Torah law recognizes it as a private domain even though the Sages treat it like a karmelit for lacking residents
A section of the Temple; it is always fully permitted
A type of public well; it is always a public domain
quiz.e: A karpef has real partitions, which is all Torah law requires for private-domain status; the Sages layered on a karmelit-like restriction only because no one actually resides there.

quiz.q: Why is the space between the pillars alongside the public domain treated as a karmelit rather than a full public domain?
o: Because it is roofed
Because the multitudes walk there, but not in a direct, unbroken path
Because it belongs to the Temple
Because no one is permitted to enter it
quiz.e: Even though people do pass through that space, their use of it is not direct and convenient the way walking down the open street is, so it remains a karmelit.

quiz.q: According to the discussion of an upright brick standing in the public domain, when is an object that lands ON TOP of it exempt from liability?
o: Only if the brick belongs to a homeowner
When the brick is at least three handbreadths high, since the multitudes don't step on top of it
Never — landing on top is always liable
Only on Shabbat afternoon
quiz.e: Once a brick is three handbreadths high, the multitudes no longer tread on its top surface, so it is treated as a domain separate from the public domain around it.

quiz.q: What does Shmuel mean by telling Rav Yehuda not to get involved in Shabbat questions 'above ten handbreadths'?
o: That the Torah does not apply above ten handbreadths
That karmelit status does not exist above a height of ten handbreadths
That priests may not enter spaces above ten handbreadths
That objects thrown above ten handbreadths are never counted
quiz.e: The Gemara concludes Shmuel meant that a karmelit 'extends up to ten' handbreadths and no further — above that height, the area is no longer governed by karmelit rules at all.

quiz.q: According to Abaye, why does digging a four-by-four handbreadth pit in the floor of a low-ceilinged house, completing its depth to ten handbreadths, permit carrying throughout the entire house?
o: Because digging always creates an exempt domain
Because the dug-out spot becomes a private domain, and the rest of the house is treated as its 'holes,' which share the private domain's status
Because digging removes the house's roof status
Because the house then becomes a karmelit
quiz.e: Abaye reasons that the pit itself qualifies as a private domain, and since holes of a private domain are universally agreed to carry the same status as the private domain, the whole house becomes fit for carrying.
